question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning given below?

To do or say something that needlessly disturbs a settled and satisfactory state of affairs.
option_2: To be in the same boat
solution_text:
The correct answer is To rock the boat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to rock the boat" means to do or say something that upsets a stable situation, or that causes trouble where all was going smoothly.

 

• Example: *The department was running quietly enough, and nobody wished to rock the boat by raising the question of the missing files.*

 

• All four alternatives are genuine boat idioms with settled and distinct meanings, so the answer must be decided by sense alone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The expression is most often used in the negative — *don't rock the boat*, *nobody wanted to rock the boat* — as a warning against disturbing a convenient arrangement.

 

• Idioms close in sense: to upset the apple cart, to open a can of worms, to put the cat among the pigeons.

 

NOTE

 

• To be in the same boat (Option 2): To be in the same difficult situation as somebody else. It describes shared circumstances, not the act of disturbing them.

 

• To miss the boat (Option 3): To lose an opportunity through being too slow. The idea is of failure to act, whereas the required meaning turns on acting when one should not.

 

• To burn one's boats (Option 4): To commit oneself irrevocably, leaving no way of retreating. The allusion is to a commander burning his ships on landing so that his men cannot turn back.

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning given below?

A person whose abilities or intentions are little known, and who may therefore surprise everybody.
solution_text:
The correct answer is A dark horse.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "a dark horse" describes a person whose qualities, abilities or intentions are not generally known, and who consequently does much better than anyone expected.

 

• Example: *He had been a dark horse throughout the trials, and few had marked him down as a possible winner.*

 

• All four alternatives belong to the horse family of idioms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The expression comes from horse racing, where a "dark" horse was one about whose form nothing was known, so that no reliable odds could be set against it.

 

• In politics a dark horse candidate is one who is little discussed beforehand and emerges unexpectedly as a compromise choice.

 

NOTE

 

• To flog a dead horse (Option 1): To waste effort on something that is already settled or hopeless — to go on arguing a case that has been decided.

 

• Straight from the horse's mouth (Option 2): Directly from the person concerned, and therefore reliable. This is a claim about the source of information, not about a person's hidden ability.

 

• To back the wrong horse (Option 3): To support the losing side or the wrong candidate. It concerns a mistaken choice, not an unknown quantity.

question: From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom "to steal someone’s thunder".
option_1: To take for oneself the credit or the attention that another had expected
option_2: To frighten a person by making a sudden and very loud noise
option_3: To speak angrily and at great length about a grievance
option_4: To give a warning of an approaching danger
solution_text:
The correct answer is To take for oneself the credit or the attention that another had expected.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to steal someone's thunder" means to take the praise, credit or attention that another person was expecting, usually by acting first or by announcing their idea before they can.

 

• Example: *The junior officer stole his chief's thunder by presenting the findings to the board a day early.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The phrase has a precise and well-attested origin. The dramatist John Dennis invented a new device for producing the sound of thunder for one of his plays in the early eighteenth century. The play failed, but the theatre went on using his thunder machine for a production of *Macbeth*. On hearing it, Dennis is said to have exclaimed that they would not run his play but would steal his thunder.

 

• Idioms close in sense: to take the wind out of someone's sails, to upstage someone.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 takes the word *thunder* literally. Idioms are always decided by the figurative sense, and this is the standard trap in questions of this kind.

 

• Option 3 describes an angry outburst, which is nearer to the idioms "to throw a fit" or "to blow one's top".

 

• Option 4 describes a warning of danger, for which the nearer expression would be "to sound the alarm".

question: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Irresistible.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is IRRESISTIBLE, meaning too attractive or too powerful to be resisted.

 

• Two features must both be got right:

 

• A double R at the start — the prefix *in-* becomes ir- before a stem beginning with *r*, giving ir + resistible.

 

• The ending is -IBLE, not *-able*.

 

• The vowel pattern of the stem is i-e-i: ir-re-sist-ible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The -ible / -able distinction is one of the most tested points in English spelling. A rough but useful rule: words whose stem is not a complete English word usually take -ible (*audible, visible, tangible, plausible, legible*), while those built on a complete word usually take -able (*comfortable, readable, dependable, agreeable*).

 

• Common -ible words worth memorising: irresistible, permissible, compatible, feasible, eligible, negligible, susceptible, accessible, responsible, flexible.

 

• The same doubling of the prefix appears in irregular, irrelevant, irrational and irreversible.

 

NOTE

 

• Irresistable (Option 1): The double r is right, but the ending is wrongly given as -able. This is by far the commonest error, and the most tempting option here.

 

• Irrisistible (Option 2): The ending is right, but an i has replaced the e of the stem *resist*.

 

• Iresistible (Option 4): Has only a single r at the start, so the prefix has not been assimilated.

question:
Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose the option "No replacement required".

The new regulation will supersede all earlier circulars issued on the subject.
solution_text:
The correct answer is No replacement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word "supersede" is already spelt correctly in the sentence, so no replacement is needed.

 

• Supersede means to take the place of; to replace something that has become out of date.

 

• The point to fix in memory is that supersede is the ONLY common English word ending in "-SEDE". Every other English word with that sound ends in -cede or -ceed:

 

• -cede: precede, concede, recede, secede, accede, intercede

 

• -ceed: exceed, proceed, succeed — only these three

 

• The word comes from Latin super ("above") + sedere ("to sit") — literally to sit above, and so to displace.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Note also proceed (verb) against procedure (noun), where the double *e* disappears; and precede (to come before) against proceed (to go forward), which are frequently confused.

 

NOTE

 

• superceed (Option 1): Wrong twice over — a c for the s, and the -ceed ending.

 

• supercede (Option 2): The commonest misspelling of the word, and by far the most tempting here. It follows the *-cede* pattern of *precede* and *concede*, which is exactly the analogy that misleads.

 

• superseed (Option 3): Keeps the s correctly but ends -seed, which is not an English ending at all in this family.

question: Choose the word that is the most appropriate synonym of the word "intransigent".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uncompromising.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Intransigent (adjective) means refusing to change one's views or to agree about anything; unwilling to compromise.

 

• Its closest synonym among the alternatives is Uncompromising.

 

• Example: *The union remained intransigent, and after four days of talks not a single clause had been settled.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from Spanish los intransigentes, the name given to a party of extremists in the Spanish Cortes of the 1870s who refused all compromise.

 

• Other synonyms: obdurate, obstinate, inflexible, adamant, unyielding, implacable.

 

NOTE

 

• Accommodating (Option 2): Means willing to fit in with the wishes of others — the direct antonym, and the principal trap here.

 

• Indifferent (Option 3): Means having no interest or concern. A useful distinction: the indifferent man does not care what is decided, while the intransigent man cares intensely and will not give way.

 

• Transient (Option 4): Means lasting only a short time. It is placed here because it resembles *intransigent* in sound; the two are unrelated in sense.

question:
There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.

The committee recommended a thorough assesment of the premises before any acquisition was approved.
solution_text:
The correct answer is assesment.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "assesment". The correct spelling is ASSESSMENT, meaning the act of judging or evaluating something, or the valuation so made.

 

• The word requires two pairs of double S: AS-SESS-MENT. The error here drops the second pair.

 

• The root is the verb assess, itself from Latin assidere, "to sit beside" — the assessor being one who sat beside the judge to fix the amount of a tax or fine.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The committee recommended a thorough assessment of the premises before any acquisition was approved.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Words of the same "double-double" family that are frequently misspelt: possess (four s's in all), address, embarrass, committee, accommodate, occurrence.

 

NOTE

 

• committee (Option 1): Correctly spelt — two m's, two t's and two e's. It is placed first precisely because it looks like the likeliest error.

 

• premises (Option 2): Correctly spelt. Note that in the sense of a building it is always plural — one speaks of *the premises*, never *a premise* meaning a building.

 

• acquisition (Option 4): Correctly spelt. Note the c before the q, which is also present in *acquire*, *acquaint* and *acquit*.

question: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Definately.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "Definately". The correct spelling is DEFINITELY, meaning certainly; without doubt.

 

• The way to get it right every time is to see the word FINITE inside it: de + FINITE + ly.

 

• Since *finite* contains an i, the third vowel of *definitely* must be i, never a.

 

• The word comes from Latin finis, "an end" — a thing is definite when its limits have been fixed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same *finis* root explains define, definition, finish, final, infinite and confine. In every one of them the vowel after *f-n* is an i.

 

• *Definately* is consistently listed among the most frequently misspelt words in English, which is why it appears so often in examinations.

 

NOTE

 

• Rendezvous (Option 1): Correctly spelt. A French borrowing meaning a meeting arranged at an agreed time and place. Note the silent z and the silent s.

 

• Camouflage (Option 2): Correctly spelt — another French borrowing, with -ou- in the middle and the ending -flage.

 

• Colleague (Option 4): Correctly spelt, with the ending -eague, as in *league*. It is often wrongly written *collegue*.

question: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to "amalgamate".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Separate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Amalgamate (verb) means to unite or combine two or more things into a single body.

 

• Its direct antonym is Separate, meaning to divide or set apart.

 

• Example: *The two banks were amalgamated in 1969 and separated again a decade later.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from amalgam, an alloy of mercury with another metal — the image being of two substances mixed until they can no longer be told apart.

 

• The noun is amalgamation, a term of constant use in company law and in banking, where the amalgamation of two institutions produces a single successor.

 

• Other antonyms: divide, disperse, sever, disunite, segregate.

 

NOTE

 

• The question is built so that three of the four options are synonyms of the key word and only one is its opposite. Spotting that shape at once saves time.

 

• Merge (Option 1): Means to combine into a single whole — the plainest synonym.

 

• Combine (Option 2): Means to join together — a second synonym.

 

• Fuse (Option 4): Means to join by melting together — a third synonym, differing only in the manner of the joining.

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of "opaque".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Transparent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Opaque (adjective) means not allowing light to pass through; not able to be seen through.

 

• Its direct antonym is Transparent, meaning allowing light to pass through so that objects behind can be clearly seen.

 

• Example: *The window had been painted over and was now opaque, though the pane beside it was perfectly transparent.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Three degrees are distinguished, and all three are examined:

 

• Transparent – light passes through and the object behind is clearly visible (clear glass, water)

 

• Translucent – light passes through but the object behind is not clearly visible (frosted glass, oiled paper)

 

• Opaque – no light passes through (wood, stone, metal)

 

• Opaque has a common figurative sense as well — *an opaque style of writing* means one that is obscure and hard to follow. In that sense too its opposite is *transparent*, meaning clear and easy to understand.

 

NOTE

 

• The question is built so that three of the four options point the same way as the key word. Recognising that shape is quicker than weighing each option.

 

• Cloudy (Option 1): Means not clear; clouded over — close in sense to opaque, not opposed to it.

 

• Murky (Option 2): Means dark and gloomy, or clouded with sediment — again a near-synonym.

 

• Turbid (Option 4): Means thick or muddy with suspended matter, as of water. A third word on the same side.

question:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The old wooden bridge could no longer _____ the weight of the loaded trucks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is bear.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct word is bear, which as a verb means to support or carry a weight, and also to endure.

 

• Completed sentence: *The old wooden bridge could no longer bear the weight of the loaded trucks.*

 

• All four options are homophones or near-homophones, so the question is decided entirely by meaning and spelling, not by sound.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bear has several senses, all tested at one time or another: to carry (*bear a burden*), to endure (*I cannot bear it*), to produce (*the tree bears fruit*), and the noun meaning the animal.

 

• Its principal parts are irregular: bear – bore – borne. Note the idiom "to bear out" (to confirm) and "to bear with" (to be patient with).

 

NOTE

 

• bare (Option 1): As an adjective, uncovered or empty; as a verb, to uncover (*he bared his head*). It cannot mean to support a weight. This is the commonest confusion of the four.

 

• bier (Option 2): A frame or stand on which a coffin is carried. Note that a bier does in fact support a weight, which makes it the subtlest distractor here — but it is a noun, and the blank requires a verb after *could no longer*.

 

• beer (Option 3): The alcoholic drink made from malt and hops. Included only for its sound.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

A person who remains unmoved by pleasure or pain, and endures misfortune without complaint.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Stoic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A stoic is a person who endures pain or hardship without showing feeling and without complaining, and who is equally unmoved by pleasure.

 

• The word comes from the Stoic school of Greek philosophy, founded by Zeno of Citium, who taught in the stoa or painted porch at Athens — from which the school takes its name.

 

• The Stoics held that a wise man should live in accordance with reason and nature, and should be indifferent to whatever fortune brings.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four options belong to a set of related but distinct attitudes, and the distinctions are the whole of the question:

 

• Stoic – indifferent to pleasure and pain alike; endures without complaint

 

• Epicurean – devoted to refined enjoyment, especially of food and drink

 

• Hedonist – holds that pleasure is the highest good and pursues it

 

• Ascetic – deliberately abstains from all pleasure, usually for religious reasons

 

• Note the difference between the stoic and the ascetic, which is the finest distinction here: the ascetic renounces pleasure as a discipline; the stoic does not renounce it, but is simply unaffected by its presence or absence.

 

NOTE

 

• Epicurean (Option 1): One who takes delight in good living. This is the opposite disposition, and the historical Epicureans were the philosophical rivals of the Stoics.

 

• Hedonist (Option 2): One who makes the pursuit of pleasure the object of life — again the reverse of indifference.

 

• Ascetic (Option 4): One who practises severe self-denial. The subtlest distractor, since an ascetic also appears untouched by comfort — but his indifference is a discipline he imposes, not a temperament he possesses.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

A speech or piece of writing in praise of a person who has recently died.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Eulogy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A eulogy is a speech or written tribute in high praise of a person, most often one delivered at a funeral or memorial service.

 

• The word comes from Greek eu ("well") + logos ("speech") — literally *good speaking*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four options here are the standard set for this question type, and the distinctions are worth learning exactly:

 

• Eulogy – a speech of praise, usually spoken at a funeral

 

• Elegy – a poem of mourning and lament for the dead. Gray's *Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard* is the classic English example

 

• Epitaph – the inscription on a tomb or gravestone

 

• Obituary – a notice of a death in a newspaper, giving an account of the person's life

 

• Note also eugenics, euphemism, euphony and euthanasia, all built on the same eu- ("good, well").

 

NOTE

 

• Elegy (Option 2): A poem of lamentation. The difference from a eulogy is the difference between mourning and praising — an elegy expresses sorrow, a eulogy admiration.

 

• Epitaph (Option 3): What is carved on the grave. It is by nature very short, and is written rather than spoken.

 

• Obituary (Option 4): A published notice recording the death and the life. It is a factual account for a newspaper, not a tribute delivered in praise.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The minister appeared wholly impervious _____ criticism from any quarter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective impervious is followed by the preposition to: *impervious to water, impervious to criticism, impervious to argument*.

 

• Completed sentence: *The minister appeared wholly impervious to criticism from any quarter.*

 

• Impervious means, literally, not allowing a fluid to pass through, and figuratively unable to be affected or influenced by something.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The figurative sense is the one usually tested. A person impervious to criticism is not merely unhurt by it — the criticism does not reach him at all.

 

• Adjectives of the same family, all taking to: immune to, insensible to, indifferent to, susceptible to, vulnerable to, resistant to, subject to, liable to, prone to.

 

NOTE

 

• from (Option 1): The natural trap, since the idea of keeping something out suggests *from*. But *impervious* follows the pattern of *immune* and *resistant*, which take to.

 

• for (Option 2): Used with *eager for, anxious for, fit for, eligible for, famous for* — a different set altogether.

 

• against (Option 3): Used with verbs and adjectives of defence and opposition — *guard against, insure against, prejudiced against* — not with *impervious*.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The fresh evidence produced by the prosecution militates _____ the accused.
solution_text:
The correct answer is against.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb militate is almost always followed by against: *to militate against a proposal, against a person, against success*.

 

• Completed sentence: *The fresh evidence produced by the prosecution militates against the accused.*

 

• To militate against something means to be a powerful factor in preventing it, or to tell strongly against it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Militate must be distinguished from mitigate, with which it is constantly confused:

 

• Militate against – to weigh against, to work to prevent (*his age militated against his selection*)

 

• Mitigate – to make less severe (*the court mitigated the sentence*). Mitigate takes a direct object and no preposition. The phrase *"mitigate against"* is always an error.

 

• Other verbs taking against: *guard against, warn against, protest against, discriminate against, insure against, retaliate against*.

 

NOTE

 

• for (Option 1): Would reverse the sense entirely, suggesting the evidence favoured the accused. *Militate* is negative by its nature and cannot govern *for*.

 

• with (Option 2): Used with *comply with, cope with, dispense with, tamper with* — not with *militate*.

 

• upon (Option 4): Used with *impose upon, prevail upon, encroach upon, act upon* — again a different set.

question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the alternative that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case the first three alternatives are not found suitable, choose the last one, "No improvement required".

Walking along the river bank, the ruined temple came into view.
option_1: Walking along with the river bank,
option_2: While we were walking along the river bank,
option_3: While walking along the river bank,
solution_text:
The correct answer is While we were walking along the river bank, the ruined temple came into view.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence contains a dangling participle (also called a misrelated participle).

 

• The rule is that a participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must describe the subject of the main clause that follows it.

 

• Here the participial phrase is *"Walking along the river bank"*, and the subject of the main clause is "the ruined temple". The sentence therefore states, absurdly, that the temple was walking along the river bank.

 

• The fault can be repaired in either of two ways: supply the true subject in the main clause, or turn the phrase into a full clause with its own subject. Option 2 takes the second course — *"While we were walking..."* — and so removes the absurdity.

 

• The alternative repair would be: *Walking along the river bank, we saw the ruined temple come into view.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Further examples of the same error, worth recognising at sight:

 

• *Having finished the report, the file was closed.* → Who finished it? Correct: *Having finished the report, he closed the file.*

 

• *Being a hot day, we stayed indoors.* → Correct: *It being a hot day, we stayed indoors.*

 

• *At the age of six, my father took me to Delhi.* → the father was not six.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 changes only the tense of the verb, from *came* to *was coming*. The participle still dangles, because the subject of the main clause remains *the temple*.

 

• Option 3 merely shifts the participial phrase to the end of the sentence. Moving it does not attach it to a proper subject; the temple is still the only candidate, so the fault is untouched.

 

• Option 4 cannot be right, since the sentence as it stands says something it plainly does not mean.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The Collector’s order reached the Tehsildar’s desk on a Friday afternoon.
A. By Monday morning the file had come back to him, endorsed by every officer who had touched it, and with no mark of any kind against the substance of the order.
B. He read it once, initialled the margin, and passed it to the clerk who dealt with land records.
C. The clerk, finding nothing in it that concerned his own section, sent it on to the revenue branch.
D. There it was read by three men in turn, each of whom added his initials neatly below the last.
S2. The order itself required a village to be moved, and not one of them had written a word about that.
solution_text:
The correct answer is BCDA.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The paragraph traces the passage of a single file through a chain of hands, and the order is fixed at every step by who holds it.

 

• B follows S1 directly. The pronoun "He" can only be the Tehsildar of S1, and B tells us what he did with the order and to whom he passed it — *the clerk*.

 

• C must follow B, because it begins "The clerk", who was introduced at the end of B, and it sends the file onward to *the revenue branch*.

 

• D must follow C, because it opens "There" — a word that needs a place already named, and the place is the revenue branch of C.

 

• A closes the sequence. It carries the time marker "By Monday morning", which must come after the Friday afternoon of S1, and it speaks of *"every officer who had touched it"* — a summing-up that presupposes the whole chain described in B, C and D.

 

• S2 then delivers the point: the order required a village to be moved, and not one of them had written a word about it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Two devices settle this question, and both are worth carrying into the examination hall:

 

• A noun introduced at the end of one sentence is picked up at the beginning of the next — Tehsildar → clerk → revenue branch. This is called lexical chaining, and it is the surest guide in narrative jumbles.

 

• A place adverb such as *"There"* cannot appear before the place it refers to.

 

NOTE

 

• DACB (Option 1): Opens with D, whose *"There"* refers to a place not yet mentioned.

 

• CBAD (Option 3): Opens with C, so *"The clerk"* appears before anyone has handed him anything, and B — in which the Tehsildar passes the file to that clerk — comes afterwards.

 

• BDCA (Option 4): Correct at both ends, but reverses C and D, so that the file reaches the revenue branch after it has already been read there. This is the most tempting of the wrong answers.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The photograph had hung in the corridor of the school for forty years without anybody looking at it.
A. Below it, on a strip of card gone brown at the edges, were eleven names and a date.
B. Then a boy stopped one afternoon to tie his shoelace, and found himself looking up at it.
C. It showed a cricket eleven, seated and standing in two rows, in caps a size too large for them.
D. Nobody in the school, he discovered over the next week, could tell him who any of them had been.
S2. He copied the eleven names into the back of his exercise book, and that was how the matter began.
solution_text:
The correct answer is BCAD.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All four alternatives begin with B, so the opening is given and the question turns entirely on the order of A, C and D.

 

• B is the hinge of the paragraph. S1 says nobody ever looked at the photograph; B supplies the word "Then" and the boy who at last did.

 

• C must come next, because it begins "It showed..." — the first description of what is in the photograph. A paragraph describes a picture only once somebody is looking at it.

 

• A follows C by a plain spatial step: having described the photograph, the eye moves to what is written "Below it" — the card with eleven names.

 

• D must be last of the four. It reports what the boy found out "over the next week", so it comes after the looking and reading, and its phrase *"who any of them had been"* refers to the eleven names introduced in A.

 

• S2 confirms the order: he copies "the eleven names" — the names of A — into his exercise book.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The paragraph moves in the natural order of noticing → seeing → reading → enquiring, and each step is longer in time than the one before: an afternoon, then a week.

 

• Where every option shares the same first letter, do not waste time on the opening. Attack instead the sentence that must come last — here D, marked by *"over the next week"* — and half the options fall away at once.

 

NOTE

 

• BACD (Option 2): Puts A before C, so the reader is shown the caption *"Below it"* before being told what the photograph itself contains.

 

• BCDA (Option 3): Places D before A, so the boy asks who *"any of them"* were before the eleven names have been mentioned — the pronoun has no antecedent.

question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the alternative that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel the first three alternatives do not improve the sentence, then choose the last one, "No improvement required".

The scheme has been in operation for the last three years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is No improvement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is already correct as it stands.

 

• The rule is a simple one and is tested constantly:

 

• FOR is used with a period or length of time — *for three years, for a fortnight, for a long while*.

 

• SINCE is used with a point of time, that is, the moment at which something began — *since 2021, since Monday, since his retirement*.

 

• Here "three years" is a length of time, so for is required, and the sentence uses it correctly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same sentence could be recast correctly with *since* only by naming a point of time: *The scheme has been in operation since 2023.*

 

• Note that with the present perfect continuous the same rule holds: *He has been waiting for two hours* / *He has been waiting since four o'clock*.

 

• "No improvement required" is a genuine answer and not a last resort. Test the underlined phrase against the rule before assuming it must be faulty.

 

NOTE

 

• since the last three years (Option 1): Wrong, and the commonest error in Indian English. *Since* cannot govern a length of time such as *three years*.

 

• from the last three years (Option 2): Wrong for the same reason. From is used with a starting point in constructions such as *from 2023 to 2026*, and does not take a period in this way.

 

• since last three years (Option 3): Wrong twice over — the misuse of *since*, and the omission of the article the before *last three years*.

question: Choose the correct synonym of the word "laconic".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Terse.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Laconic (adjective) means using very few words; brief to the point of seeming abrupt.

 

• Its closest synonym among the alternatives is Terse, which means concise and to the point.

 

• Example: *Asked to explain the delay, he gave a laconic reply of four words and said nothing further.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from Laconia, the region of ancient Greece of which Sparta was the capital. The Spartans were famous for their extreme brevity of speech. When Philip of Macedon sent word that if he entered Laconia he would raze it to the ground, the Spartans are said to have replied with a single word: "If."

 

• Other synonyms: concise, succinct, pithy, curt, brief, sparing of words.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbose (Option 1): Means using far more words than are needed — the direct antonym, and the principal trap here. Its companions are *prolix*, *long-winded* and *garrulous*.

 

• Melodious (Option 2): Means pleasant-sounding. It concerns the quality of a sound, not the quantity of words.

 

• Fluent (Option 3): Means speaking easily and smoothly. A fluent speaker may be very brief or very long-winded — the word says nothing about length, only about ease.

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:

 

"Ozymandias" is a sonnet of fourteen lines in which almost nothing is described at first hand. The poem opens with a frame: the speaker tells us only that he met a traveller from an antique land, and the whole of what follows is the traveller’s report. This device of the reported narrator sets the ruin at two removes from the reader, and is the first of the poem’s several distancings. What the traveller describes is a wreck — two vast legs of stone standing in the desert, and near them a shattered face half sunk in the sand, its frown and its sneer of cold command still legible after three thousand years. The poem then makes its most interesting turn. Those expressions survive, we are told, because the sculptor read them well and stamped them upon lifeless stone; so that what has outlasted the king is not his power at all, but the eye of the anonymous workman who once observed him. On the pedestal stand the words commanding the mighty to look upon his works and despair. Around the pedestal there is nothing whatever — the boundless and bare sands stretch away on every side. The irony is nowhere stated; it is built. The inscription and the emptiness are simply set beside each other and left to collide in the reader’s mind. The subject of the poem is therefore not merely the fall of one tyrant but the fate of every claim made against time, and its method is to say nothing at all, and to let a boast and a desert do the arguing.

 

Which device does the passage identify at the opening of the poem?
option_1: Apostrophe, since the poet addresses the statue directly
option_2: A frame, in which a reported narrator relates the whole of what follows
option_3: Hyperbole, by which the size of the ruin is deliberately exaggerated
option_4: Alliteration, which gives the opening lines their musical quality
solution_text:
The correct answer is A frame, in which a reported narrator relates the whole of what follows.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states it in the second sentence: *"The poem opens with a frame: the speaker tells us only that he met a traveller from an antique land, and the whole of what follows is the traveller's report."*

 

• It gives the device its name — the reported narrator — and explains its effect: it *"sets the ruin at two removes from the reader"*.

 

• The two removes are worth counting. The reader hears the speaker; the speaker heard the traveller; the traveller saw the ruin.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The passage calls this *"the first of the poem's several distancings"*, which signals that distance — in time, in space and in narration — is a theme the passage will return to.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 names apostrophe, which is direct address to an absent person or a thing. The poem's speaker addresses nobody; he reports.

 

• Option 3 names hyperbole. The passage does describe the legs as *"vast"*, but it nowhere suggests exaggeration — and in any case this is not what the poem opens with.

 

• Option 4 names alliteration. The passage makes no claim about the musicality of the opening lines.

option_1: Because the stone from which the statue was carved was unusually hard
option_2: Because the desert sands preserved the face from wind and rain

solution_text:

• The passage gives the reason exactly: *"Those expressions survive, we are told, because the sculptor read them well and stamped them upon lifeless stone."*

 

• Two things are being claimed at once, and both matter. The sculptor read the king correctly — that is, he understood his character — and he stamped what he had read on the stone with sufficient skill for it to last.

 

• The survival is therefore credited to an act of observation and craft, not to any property of the material or the climate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

• The verb "read" is doing unusual work here. One reads a text; the sculptor is said to have read a face. The passage uses the word to make the sculptor's perception a kind of literacy — which prepares the point made in the following question.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 offers a property of the material. The passage calls the stone *"lifeless"*, which is the opposite of crediting it with the achievement.

 

• Option 2 offers a property of the climate. The sands are mentioned in the passage, but only as what surrounds the ruin and as the emptiness that produces the irony — never as a preservative.

What does the passage identify as the subject of the poem?
option_1: The skill of ancient Egyptian sculpture and the techniques by which it was made
option_2: The hardships endured by travellers crossing the deserts of an antique land
option_3: The duty of poets to record the deeds of kings before they are forgotten

• Option 1 makes the poem a study of technique. The sculptor's skill is discussed, but as evidence for the poem's irony, not as its subject.

question: इंपीरियल बैंक ऑफ इंडिया का रूपांतरण करके भारतीय स्टेट बैंक का गठन किस वर्ष हुआ था?
solution_text:
सही उत्तर 1955 है।

 

महत्वपूर्ण बिंदु

 

• भारतीय स्टेट बैंक का गठन 1 जुलाई 1955 को भारतीय स्टेट बैंक अधिनियम, 1955 के अंतर्गत इंपीरियल बैंक ऑफ इंडिया का अधिग्रहण करके किया गया था। (भारतीय स्टेट बैंक — 1955)

 

• यह कदम ए.डी. गोरेवाला की अध्यक्षता वाली अखिल भारतीय ग्रामीण साख सर्वेक्षण समिति की सिफारिश पर उठाया गया था, जिसका मत था कि बैंकिंग को ग्रामीण क्षेत्रों तक पहुँचाने के लिए राज्य-भागीदारी एवं राज्य-प्रायोजित बैंक आवश्यक है।

 

• इंपीरियल बैंक ऑफ इंडिया का गठन स्वयं 1921 में तीन प्रेसीडेंसी बैंकों — बंगाल (1806), बंबई (1840) तथा मद्रास (1843) — के विलय से हुआ था।

 

• एसबीआई आज भारत का सबसे बड़ा सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र का बैंक है, जिसका मुख्यालय मुंबई में है।

 

अतः सही उत्तर विकल्प 1 है।

 

अतिरिक्त जानकारी

 

• भारतीय बैंकिंग के इतिहास के प्रमुख पड़ाव:

• 1806 – बैंक ऑफ बंगाल, पहला प्रेसीडेंसी बैंक

 

• 1921 – इंपीरियल बैंक ऑफ इंडिया का गठन

 

• 1935 – भारतीय रिज़र्व बैंक की स्थापना, हिल्टन यंग आयोग की सिफारिश पर

 

• 1955 – भारतीय स्टेट बैंक का गठन

 

• 1969 – 14 प्रमुख बैंकों का राष्ट्रीयकरण; 1980 – 6 और बैंकों का

 

नोट

 

• 1949 (विकल्प 2): यह बैंककारी विनियमन अधिनियम का वर्ष है, तथा इसी वर्ष आरबीआई का राष्ट्रीयकरण भी हुआ था — यह वास्तविक बैंकिंग पड़ाव है और यहाँ सबसे प्रबल भ्रामक विकल्प।
